title: New film starring Helen Mirren explores Patricia Highsmith's later years
content: A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes. “But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”.
summary: Publisher Otto Penzler recalls his 1984 meeting with Patricia Highsmith, noting her taciturn nature and lack of interest in readers. A new film starring Helen Mirren examines the author's later life and reputation for being rude and eccentric.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Emma Fogarty, Rare Skin Condition, Flies on Private Jet to London for Documentary Premiere
content:
HBO arranged a private jet from Dublin to London for the premiere of the new documentary The Slightest Touch, transporting star Emma Fogarty, who has the rare genetic skin condition epidermolysis bullosa (EB). The film features Colin Farrell, but the special travel arrangement was made for Fogarty because taking a commercial flight would have been physically impossible for her. A publicist working on the project noted that this was a rare instance where emitting carbon could be done with a clear conscience.

Fogarty, who is 42 years old, was told by a doctor at the time of her diagnosis that she was unlikely to survive a week. EB causes the proteins that hold skin layers together to be missing or faulty, resulting in skin as fragile as a butterfly’s wings. Minor impacts can cause her skin to tear or blister, and 80% of her body is currently without skin, requiring bandages to protect the wounds.

The documentary tells the story of Fogarty’s life and her lifelong bond with Farrell, including her completion of a marathon with his assistance. The film also explores why Farrell opened up about parenthood, highlighting the extraordinary nature of their relationship.
summary: Emma Fogarty, who has the rare genetic skin condition epidermolysis bullosa, was flown on a private jet from Dublin to London for the premiere of the documentary featuring Colin Farrell. The flight was necessary because a commercial flight would have been physically impossible for her due to her fragile skin.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Midnight Diner Season 6 Drops on Netflix, Quietly Buried by Platform
content:
The sixth season of the Japanese drama Midnight Diner has recently been released on Netflix, marking the show’s return after a seven-year absence. The series, which is based on Yarō Abe’s long-running manga, has been a staple of Japanese television since 2009. The delay in its release was partly attributed to uncertainty regarding the pandemic’s impact on small eateries.

In the opening scene, the protagonist, known as the Master and played by Kaoru Kobayashi, appears morose as his Tokyo eatery, typically open from midnight to 7 am, stands empty. He notes that customers are staying home due to the coronavirus, a situation described as an ironic start for a drama centered on a bustling late-night restaurant.

Despite the show’s thoughtful stillness and critical acclaim, it has received little attention. The article suggests that the release has been overshadowed by other content, attributing this lack of visibility to Netflix’s apparent reluctance to market non-English series. This approach has reportedly caused the platform to overlook other remarkable Japanese television productions.
summary: The sixth season of Midnight Diner follows Master Kaoru Kobayashi as his Tokyo eatery, open from midnight to 7am, remains empty due to Covid‑19. Netflix quietly released the season, but it has been buried by the platform’s limited promotion of non‑English series.

title: DCU’s James Gunn and Peter Safran fired, Jeremy Latcham appointed
content:
James Gunn and Peter Safran, the co-CEOs of DC Studios, have been fired, marking a significant disruption to the recently launched DC Universe (DCU). According to the report, the duo will reportedly remain with the studio as filmmakers. Jeremy Latcham, described as another former Marvel executive, has been appointed as the new boss of the division.

The DCU initiative was originally designed in 2022 to replace the DC Extended Universe (DCEU) with a fresh start, aiming to clear away previous tonal inconsistencies and false starts. The strategy heavily relied on hiring Gunn, whose creative vision was intended to drive the new slate of superhero films. However, four years later, the article states that this plan is now in tatters following the leadership change.

The departure leaves the future direction of the DCU uncertain, with the source noting that nobody seems to know the current plan. The article also references David Ellison, whose Skydance empire recently acquired Warner, describing the situation as chaotic. This leadership shakeup is characterized as one of the biggest disasters to hit superhero movies in recent years, raising questions about whether the DCU can ever get back on track.
summary: James Gunn and Peter Safran, the DC Studios CEO and co‑CEO, were fired this week. Former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham has been named the new head of DC Studios.

title: Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta
content:
Thomas Frank has taken the helm at Crystal Palace with a clear set of priorities.  In a brief outline of his first season, he has identified three key tasks: lifting the team’s mood, tightening the defence and energising players Sarr and Mateta.  

Frank’s arrival follows his dismissal from Tottenham Hotspur in February, after which he received a reported £8 million payoff.  He kept a low profile in the months that followed, describing the experience at Spurs as “traumatic” in conversations with sources close to the 53‑year‑old.  He had even promised his wife, Nanna, a year’s sabbatical, but the opportunity to lead Palace prompted him to return sooner.  

In early June, Frank broke his silence with a statement released by the League Managers Association.  The announcement noted that he would cover the World Cup for the BBC—directly competing with former Spurs coach Ange Postecoglou, who works for ITV—before taking time to experience the Tour de France, a lifelong passion.  During his nine‑year spell at Brentford, Frank usually travelled to training and home matches from his East Sheen home, but he also cycled occasionally to clear his head.
summary: Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta.

title: Bukayo Saka receives Sócrates award at Ballon d’Or ceremony for humanitarian work
content: By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience Valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria in 2022. “I remember thinking: ‘Is this really Bukayo writing us an email?’” says the president of BigShoe, a non-profit organisation based in Frankfurt that has helped more than 10,000 children worldwide. “But that’s how he is. He’s always asking what more we can do.” Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work. She got the words from Byiringiro, a 14-year-old from Rwanda who had his eyesight restored after having surgery thanks to BigShoe’s initiative.
summary: Arsenal forward Bukayo Saka was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian efforts. He had earlier contacted the Frankfurt‑based non‑profit BigShoe, and the letter he read onstage was supplied by Byiringiro, a 14‑year‑old from Rwanda whose eyesight was restored through the charity’s initiative.

title: Tuchel defends England's 3-2 win over Spain, cites Mexico reloaded comparison
content: ‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2. The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before. The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.
summary: Thomas Tuchel said England would not change their playing style after a 3-2 win over Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium. He compared the victory to Mexico's 3-2 last‑16 win at Azteca, noting defensive substitutions that left three centre‑backs and highlighted Jarell Quansah and red cards.
author: Guardian Sport

title: UN asked to review FIFA's climate status over Aramco deal and tournament expansion
content:
The United Nations has been asked to review Fifa’s status as a signatory to the Sports for Climate Action Framework, with complainants alleging the football governing body has a “record of failure” on climate action. This initiative encourages sporting organizations to collaborate toward a climate-resilient future, requiring signatories to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2030 and partner with stakeholders for joint climate action.

Critics are questioning Fifa’s “sincerity” in meeting these emissions pledges, citing its partnership with oil giant Aramco, a major sponsor of the organization, as well as its tournament expansion. Under the framework’s rules, a signatory’s status can be revoked if concerns arise regarding their sincerity or ability to participate in the agreed-upon climate commitments.
summary: Complainants have asked the United Nations to review FIFA's status as a signatory to the Sports for Climate Action Framework, citing a record of failure on climate action. The groups question FIFA's sincerity in meeting emissions pledges due to its sponsorship deal with oil giant Aramco and tournament expansion.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Cricket player uses 'walker' reputation to cheat in semi‑final
content: Cricket always celebrates sportsmanship and condemns cheating, but where exactly is the line between the two? I once played in a one-day semi-final. We were in a very tight spot when I edged the ball to the keeper. I didn’t walk. The opposition couldn’t believe it. They crowded around me, furious, and I was getting plenty of abuse. I managed to get a single and when I reached the other end the umpire said: “You didn’t nick that did you? You are a walker.” “Yep, that’s right,” I replied.
summary: A cricket player in a one‑day semi‑final edged a ball to the keeper but did not walk, leading to abuse from the opposition. The umpire called him a “walker” and he confirmed the claim.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Irish boxer Lee Reeves dies aged 31 after coma
content: Irish boxer Lee Reeves died at the age of 31, three months after sustaining serious injuries during a bout in Dublin. The death was announced by his promoter, Queensberry.
summary: Irish boxer Lee Reeves has died at the age of 31, three months after suffering serious injuries in a bout in Dublin. His death was announced by his promoter, Queensberry.
author: BBC Sport

title: Briton Emmanuel Oyebadejo, medicine student and basketball player, now on brink of NFL
content: Emmanuel Oyebadejo, a Briton who was originally studying medicine and playing basketball, is now on the brink of making British history in the NFL. He was initially scouted while attending games as a spectator.
summary: Emmanuel Oyebadejo was supposed to be studying medicine and playing basketball. How did he become tipped to make British history in a completely different sport?
author: BBC Sport

title: Pique says Owono did not deserve 12‑match ban after Tenerife death
content: FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique stated that goalkeeper Jesus Owono did not merit the 12-match suspension imposed after his challenge. The incident resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
summary: FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique said goalkeeper Jesus Owono did not deserve the 12‑match suspension he received. The suspension followed Owono's challenge that caused the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
author: BBC Sport

title: G7 economic optimism falls to Great Recession levels, Gallup survey shows
content: A new Gallup survey indicates that economic optimism among residents of Group of Seven (G7) countries has fallen to its lowest level since the late 2000s Great Recession. The data shows that a median of 22 percent of G7 residents aged 15 and older reported that their local economic conditions were improving.
summary: G7 economic optimism falls to Great Recession levels, Gallup survey shows.
author: The Hill

title: Nvidia board not considering Jensen Huang's return as CEO
content: Nvidia’s Board of Directors is not considering Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, according to a source familiar with the matter who spoke to The Hill. This comes shortly after Huang stepped down from his role amid a national security scandal, which prompted petitions for his reinstatement. President Trump stated on Monday that he “certainly wouldn’t mind” if Huang returned to the position.
summary: Nvidia’s Board of Directors is not weighing Jensen Huang’s return as CEO. Petitions for his return circulated after his stepping down amid a national security scandal, and President Trump said he would not mind if Huang returned as CEO.
author: The Hill

title: Customers at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo report account access issues after Outlook outage
content: Customers at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, and Truist reported difficulties accessing their accounts following a major Microsoft Outlook outage. A J.P. Morgan-Chase Bank spokesperson told The Hill that the bank’s systems were experiencing a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems.
summary: Customers at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U. S.
author: The Hill

title: Campaign for Accountability Files Complaint Against U.S. Attorney Reitz Over Threats to Senators
content:
Campaign for Accountability, a left‑leaning watchdog group, filed a complaint with the Texas Bar against U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz of the Southern District of Texas. The complaint concerns Reitz’s threats directed at Senators Elizabeth Warren (D‑Mass.) and Richard Blumenthal (D‑Conn.).

The complaint alleges that some of Reitz’s remarks about the senators violated three rules outlined in the Texas Bar.
summary: Campaign for Accountability, a left-leaning watchdog group, filed a complaint with the Texas Bar against U. S.
author: The Hill

title: Vice President Vance mocks Democrats over 'soft on China' claim about Trump
content: Vice President Vance mocked Democrats who accused President Trump of being “soft on China” amid criticism of the administration’s handling of the Nvidia scandal. “Now again, I find it just hysterical that the Democrats are accusing Donald Trump of being soft on China,” Vance said during an interview with Fox News. “When it comes to…
summary: Vice President Vance mocked Democrats who accused President Trump of being 'soft on China' during a Fox News interview. The remarks came amid criticism of the administration's handling of the Nvidia scandal.
author: The Hill

title: Senate Republicans unveil $1.1T defense appropriations bill for FY2027
content: Senate Republicans unveiled a nearly $1.1 trillion defense appropriations bill for fiscal year 2027 on Monday. The proposal adds tens of billions of dollars to programs that were originally part of the Pentagon’s $350 billion reconciliation request. It also shifts close to $69 billion from the reconciliation package into the base budget, a move that signals skepticism about the earlier request.
summary: Senate Republicans unveiled a nearly $1.1 trillion defense appropriations bill for fiscal year 2027 that includes tens of billions in funding for programs originally part of the Pentagon’s $350 billion reconciliation request. The bill also moved close to $69 billion from reconciliation to the base budget.
author: The Hill

title: Comer Announces Bid for Kentucky Governor
content: Rep. James Comer (R‑Ky.) announced on Monday that he is running for Kentucky’s governor’s mansion. He said serving the state is a calling and that Kentucky needs a leader whose policies will bring growth and good‑paying jobs, noting the recent election cycle in which Democrats gained control of Congress and a historic number of state legislatures.
summary: Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) announced a bid for Kentucky’s governor’s mansion following an election cycle where Democrats took control of Congress and a historic number of state legislatures.
author: The Hill

title: Peltola expands lead over Sullivan in latest Alaska ballot drop
content: Alaska’s Division of Elections released a ballot drop showing former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) leading incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R) in the last Senate race to be called from the November midterms. Peltola had 141,637 votes, while Sullivan had 130,162, indicating an expanded lead.
summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) continues to pull ahead of incumbent Sen.
author: The Hill

title: Affordability drives midterm voters, elevates childcare to top issue
content: Affordability dominated the midterm election agenda, and childcare costs rose to prominence as a key concern. Childcare expenses have surged, imposing a significant financial burden on U.S. families. Advocates note that the issue, once peripheral, became a major political topic during the midterms.
summary: Childcare costs have surged, putting a major financial burden on U. S.
author: NPR Politics

title: Trump travels to Asia for meetings with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout
content: President Trump is traveling to Asia to meet with Chinese leader Xi and Russian leader Putin, a visit occurring amidst fallout involving Nvidia. The trip to China marks his second visit to the country this year and takes place as the president and his party face widespread voter backlash following the recent midterm elections.
summary: Trump is heading to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin as Nvidia fallout looms. The China trip is his second this year and comes as the president and his party face widespread backlash from voters in the recent midterm elections.
author: NPR Politics

title: Zoe Williams: Why refugees are rarely seen as fully human in media
content:
Zoe Williams, a Guardian columnist, reflects on the changing narrative surrounding refugees in current affairs, arguing that they are increasingly rarely depicted as fully human individuals. In her piece, she notes that the understanding of refugees as complex people, motivated by desires to build new lives or reclaim what was theirs, appears to have been lost. Instead, refugees are often categorized into specific archetypes: the desperate victim, the potential criminal, or the hero overcoming odds, a narrative typically reserved for second-generation diaspora members speaking about their parents. Additionally, they are frequently discussed en masse, stripped of individual traits and evaluated solely based on a host state’s capacity to accommodate them and the duration of their stay.

Williams highlights a recent screening of the film Seize the Summit as an example of a different perspective. The film follows four refugees attempting to reach the top of Kilimanjaro. The screening was organized by Hanya, a recent MA graduate from Goldsmiths, who was set to chair a panel discussion with Williams. During their preparation, Hanya stated that the filmmaker, Arwa Damon, aimed to "mainstream the idea of the refugee as a human being." Williams describes this statement as stark, noting that she and Hanya both laughed upon hearing it. The article positions this film as offering a truer, more nuanced view of refugees compared to the reductive categories often found in mainstream media.
summary: Zoe Williams argues that current affairs storytelling often reduces refugees to stereotypes such as victims, criminals, or heroes rather than complex individuals. She highlights a new film, Seize the Summit, which follows four refugees climbing Kilimanjaro, as an effort to mainstream the idea of refugees as human beings.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Experimental orchard at Myrtle Farm aims to help UK cider industry adapt to climate change
content:
Farmers are turning to science and nature to help orchards adapt to changing temperatures, rainfall and pests. At Myrtle Farm in Somerset, thousands of apple trees are planted in rows of 100. Over the past year each tree endured the same wet winter and long summer drought, and researchers are analysing how the different trees responded. The findings could influence apple growing and cider flavour for decades.

Myrtle Farm is the site of Thatchers Cider, which this year recorded its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122‑year history. The farm also operates an experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, with each 100‑tree row grown from a different apple variety. The trials aim to determine whether such diversity can make future harvests more consistent and predictable.

During this year’s harvest, two apple varieties were ripe from mid‑August to November at Myrtle Farm. The data from these trees will feed into the orchard’s long‑term research, offering a potential path forward for the UK cider industry as climate conditions continue to shift.
summary: Myrtle Farm in Somerset is analyzing 3,800 experimental apple trees to determine how different varieties respond to shifting weather patterns. The trials aim to ensure future harvests remain consistent and predictable despite the challenges of a deepening climate emergency.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Australia Named 'Fossil of the Day' as COP31 Negotiations Face Divisions
content:
The first draft of the COP31 agreement is under intense scrutiny as the negotiations enter their final days.  Delegates report thorny divisions, with the draft attempting to “draw out parties” on areas of disagreement rather than reach a comprehensive settlement.

Australia, the co‑host of the conference, was named Climate Action Network’s (CAN) “Fossil of the Day” yesterday.  Campaigners described the country’s actions as a masterclass in climate hypocrisy, noting that Australia presides over the climate talks while approving new polluting projects.  CAN awards the title each day to a nation perceived to block progress.
summary: Australia was dubbed “Fossil of the Day” by Climate Action Network for its climate hypocrisy during COP31. The award highlighted Australia’s role as COP31 co-host while it signs off on polluting projects.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Scientists identify likely cause of typhoid fever's deadliest complication
content:
Scientists have identified the likely cause of typhoid fever’s deadliest complication.  

The disease, an ancient scourge that remains deadly in the developing world, has been described in detail for more than a century, yet its reasons for lethality were unknown. Yale researchers now provide an explanation.
summary: Typhoid fever is an ancient scourge that remains all too deadly in the developing world today. Yale researchers now have an answer.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Daytime brain waves resembling deep sleep could explain hallucinations in Parkinson's disease
content:
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive brain disorder that damages dopamine‑producing neurons, leading to worsening symptoms over time. The disease is most commonly known for motor difficulties such as tremors, stiffness, poor balance, and slowed movements.

Beyond movement, Parkinson’s also affects cognition, perception, and sleep. Caregivers and health‑care workers frequently report that patients experience cognitive decline, excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), and perceptual distortions, which can significantly reduce quality of life.

These non‑motor symptoms highlight the broader impact of Parkinson’s disease on daily functioning and underscore the importance of comprehensive care that addresses both motor and non‑motor challenges.
summary: Parkinson's disease damages dopamine‑producing neurons and causes motor difficulties such as tremors, stiffness, poor balance and slow movements. The disease also leads to cognitive decline, excessive daytime sleepiness, and perceptual distortions that affect quality of life.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Science Tokyo shows matrix stiffness drives hepatic stellate cells toward fibrosis or regeneration
content:
Researchers from Science Tokyo examined how the stiffness of the extracellular matrix affects hepatic stellate cells during liver injury. They studied soft and stiff environments to assess the cells’ responses.

The study found that soft conditions promote regeneration‑associated cellular states, while stiff conditions drive fibrosis‑associated gene expression.
summary: Researchers from Science Tokyo studied how matrix stiffness affects hepatic stellate cells during liver injury. They found that soft matrix conditions promote regeneration-associated states, whereas stiff conditions drive fibrosis-associated gene expression.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Review shows kangaroo care reduces deaths and infections in preterm babies
content: A recent review found that kangaroo care—holding low‑birth‑weight and preterm babies skin‑to‑skin against a caregiver’s chest, providing frequent exclusive breastfeeding, and discharging them early when appropriate—probably reduces deaths and serious infections compared with conventional neonatal care. The benefit was especially clear in low‑resource settings.
summary: Kangaroo care, which involves holding low‑birth‑weight and preterm babies skin‑to‑skin, providing frequent exclusive breastfeeding, and discharging them early when appropriate, probably reduces deaths and serious infections compared with conventional neonatal care. The effect was especially clear in low‑resource settings.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Daily iron tablets cut anemia risk in children and teens, study shows
content: A review published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews found that giving children and adolescents a daily iron tablet significantly reduces the risk of iron deficiency anemia. The analysis included 114 studies with more than 50,000 participants and reported little to no effect on several common illnesses.
summary: A review of 114 studies with over 50,000 participants found that giving children and adolescents a daily iron tablet significantly reduces the risk of iron deficiency anemia. The review, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, reported little to no effect on several common illnesses.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Immune cell state may explain cytomegalovirus evasion of body's defenses
content: A recent study suggests that the state of immune cells may help explain how human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) evades the body’s defenses. HCMV is a major global health burden that causes lifelong infection in humans. It is the leading infectious cause of developmental disabilities in children and can be life‑threatening to individuals with a weakened immune system, such as transplant patients. Despite 70 years of research on HCMV, the mechanisms by which the virus evades immune control remain incompletely understood.
summary: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a major global health burden that causes lifelong infection in humans. It is the leading infectious cause of developmental disabilities in children and can be life-threatening to individuals with a weakened immune system, for example, in transplant patients.
author: Medical Xpress

title: US flu cases rise as virus kills two children
content: U.S. flu activity is increasing, with outpatient visits for influenza‑like illness rising to 3.2% of total visits, above the 2.9% national baseline and signaling the start of flu season. While cases of respiratory syncytial virus and COVID‑19 remain low, the virus has claimed the lives of two children.
summary: US flu cases rise as virus kills two children.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Nanotechnology enables ultrathin flat optics for smaller imaging systems
content: Advances in nanotechnology are enabling researchers to engineer materials at scales smaller than the wavelength of light. These ultrathin optical components offer new methods for controlling light behavior, providing an alternative to traditional optical systems that have historically relied on lenses, mirrors, and other shape-based components.
summary: Advances in nanotechnology allow researchers to engineer materials at scales smaller than the wavelength of light. These ultrathin components offer new ways to control light behavior, moving beyond traditional lenses and mirrors.
author: Phys.org

title: BC Ferries vessel strikes and kills humpback whale
content: A humpback whale was fatally injured after a BC Ferries vessel struck it on October 18. The incident, which occurred during a ferry crossing, turned an awe-inspiring wildlife sighting into a disturbing experience for passengers aboard the boat.
summary: A BC Ferries vessel struck and fatally injured a humpback whale on Oct. 18. The incident disturbed passengers who had been observing the whale from the boat.
author: Phys.org

title: Sun, Earth, Jupiter, and White Dwarfs May Trap Dark Matter
content: Dark matter remains undetected by direct experiments, partly because its slower-moving particles may produce signals too faint for current detectors. However, these particles could be captured by massive bodies such as the Sun, Earth, Jupiter, and white dwarfs. As they accumulate inside such objects, they might generate observable effects that existing instruments could detect.
summary: Dark matter continues to evade direct detection. Slower-moving particles might be captured by planets and stars, accumulating inside them and potentially producing detectable effects.
author: Phys.org

title: 19-Year Study Finds Longer Naps Linked to Higher Mortality in Older Adults
content:
A 19-year study involving 1,338 older adults indicates that napping habits may signal underlying health issues. Researchers found that longer and more frequent daytime sleep is associated with higher mortality rates. Specifically, each additional hour of napping was linked to a 13% increase in the risk of death.

The timing of naps also appeared to influence outcomes. The study revealed that morning nappers faced a 30% greater risk of death compared to those who napped in the afternoon. These findings suggest that both the duration and frequency of naps could serve as potential indicators of health status in older populations.
summary: 19-Year Study Finds Longer Naps Linked to Higher Mortality in Older Adults.
author: Science Daily

title: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
content: Scientists have identified hidden ecosystems within metal-rich rocks on the Pacific Ocean floor, where researchers examined 244 nodules and discovered more than 4,100 animals residing in their cracks and cavities. These microscopic habitats host unique animal communities that differ from those found in the surrounding seafloor mud. The rocks, which take millions of years to form, now face potential threats from deep-sea mining operations aimed at extracting valuable metals.
summary: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud.
author: Science Daily

title: Ancient virus in chimp genome silences LINC00662, a gene active in human brain development
content:
Scientists at Lund University have identified a potential mechanism for a key difference in human brain development. They discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene named LINC00662. In contrast, this gene remains active in humans, where it appears to play an important role in early brain development.

This finding suggests that a virus infecting chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape how human brains develop. The research highlights a distinct genetic variation between humans and their closest relatives, linking an ancient viral infection to the evolutionary divergence of brain development processes.
summary: Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662. The gene remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists control magnetic spin in a single atom’s nucleus with radio waves
content: Scientists have unexpectedly discovered how to control the magnetic spin inside a single atom's nucleus using radio waves, overturning prior assumptions about atomic behavior. The breakthrough could pave the way for more reliable quantum memory, although researchers are still trying to understand why it works.
summary: Scientists discovered how to control the magnetic spin inside a single atom's nucleus using radio waves. The breakthrough could lead to more reliable quantum memory, though researchers are still trying to understand why it works.
author: Science Daily

title: Voyager 1 Nears One Light-Day from Earth, Experts Discuss Journey
content:
NASA launched the Voyager 1 and 2 probes almost 50 years ago to explore the outer reaches of the solar system.  Voyager 1, now the farthest human‑made object from Earth, is approaching a distance of one light‑day from our planet.  

In the Guardian Science Podcast, host Madeleine Finlay interviews Jim Bell, a planetary scientist and professor at Arizona State University’s School of Earth and Space Exploration.  Bell discusses the mission’s seismic impact on our understanding of the solar system and speculates on Voyager 1’s future trajectory now that it has left the heliosphere.  The episode is supported by the Guardian (theguardian.com) and appears on the SciencePod channel.
summary: Voyager 1 is about to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, making it the farthest human‑made object. Planetary scientist Jim Bell explains the mission's seismic impact and Voyager 1's future path after leaving the heliosphere.
author: Guardian Science

title: ISS Astronaut Captures Lightning as Fireworks Across South China Sea
content: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Tossing Fireworks from Cloud… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search October 28, 2026 For astronauts on the International Space Station, looking back to Earth at night can be as dazzling as looking outward toward the stars. In an essay for Air & Space magazine, Donald Pettit, a NASA astronaut and dedicated photographer, described the “spectacular” view of Earth at night visible from the station. Cities and civilization, he wrote, looked “like tendrils outlined with the glimmer of a Broadway marquee.” Intense, colorful lights cast by clusters of fishing boats across darkened oceans reminded him of “a constellation of stars” forming “unfamiliar members of the Zodiac.” NASA astronaut Sally Ride —the first American woman to fly in space—also marveled at the “indescribable” sights of Earth from orbit. Lightning was among the most spectacular, she noted in an essay for the same magazine. “On Earth, people see lightning from below the clouds. In orbit, we see it from above,” she wrote. “Bolts of lightning are diffused by the clouds into bursting balls of light. Sometimes, when a storm extends hundreds of miles, it looks like a transcontinental brigade is tossing fireworks from cloud to cloud.” All three phenomena—city lights, fishing fleets, and lightning—were on display when the space station passed over the South China Sea near Borneo at 14:20 UTC (9:20 p. M. Western Indonesian Time) on October 28, 2026. When an astronaut captured this scene with a Nikon Z9 camera, several overshooting tops bubbled up from thunderstorms, including two illuminated by lightning flashes. These tall, domelike protrusions rise above a thunderstorm’s anvil and sometimes into the stratosphere, indicating strong updrafts and intense storms. The lights of Singapore, a city-state of 6.2 million people, appear on the left side of the image, with the curving Singapore Strait separating the city from Batam and Bintan islands to the south. The cluster of blue lights west of Singapore, reminiscent of the Pleiades, or Seven Sisters, was likely produced by fishing boats using bright lights to attract squid or schooling fish such as sardines or anchovies. Offshore to the northwest, the scattered orange points are likely gas flares. For many astronauts, it’s the sight of lightning that lingers. “Like fireflies in the night, lightning is my favorite sight from space,” said NASA astronaut Anil Menon in a video of Earth’s darkened limb that he posted on X, where pinpoints of lightning flicker almost constantly. Lightning is hard to capture and share, he added, but the video offers the best representation he’s seen. “It’s unchanged, at real speed, and shows the vast reach of storms and lightning across earth, plus the rapid flashes that dance across the horizon.” NASA scientists estimate that there are 2,000 thunderstorms occurring on Earth at any one moment, producing nearly 60 flashes per second—roughly 5 million flashes per day. Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-250951 was acquired on October 28, 2026, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 14 millimeters. It is provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. The image was taken by a member of the Expedition 75 crew. The image has been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed. The International Space Station Program supports the laboratory as part of the ISS National Lab to help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the Internet. Additional images taken by astronauts and cosmonauts can be viewed at the NASA/JSC Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth. Story by Adam Voiland. title: APOD November 17, 2026 features Milky Way and aurora image from Norway
content: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 17 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Original Annotated Milky Way versus Aurora Explanation: Are these two giant arches battling for control of the sky? No, but it sure looks like it! The arch on the left is the central band of our Milky Way Galaxy, an ancient system of stars, gas, and dust that predates our Earth and is very far away. The arch on the right, by contrast, is an auroral ribbon that is only hours old, composed of energized atoms and molecules, and is close by — right in Earth’s upper atmosphere. These chance-superposed titan s have our Sun in common, a stellar member of the Milky Way that ejects energetic particles which create aurora s. Far behind the middle of the auroral arch is the Big Dipper. Even farther in the distance is the Andromeda galaxy — the bright spot near the top of the frame, just left of center. The featured image was taken about a month ago from Kvaløya in northern Norway.
